goal: Decide what mistake would cost more for your classifier: a false alarm or a missed case. Write that down before you compute anything.

steps.label: Decide which mistake costs more
steps.why: Metrics only make sense once you know which error hurts.
do: Think about your Day 2 classifier as if a business depended on it.
A false alarm: it says 'yes' when the truth is 'no'. A missed case: it says 'no' when the truth is 'yes'.
Decide which would cost more in your scenario and why.
steps.see: One sentence naming the costlier mistake.

checkpoint.prompt: Which mistake costs more for your classifier, and why?
checkpoint.placeholder: Example: A missed case. If this were a defect detector, shipping a bad part costs more than re-checking a good one.

steps.label: Test on 20 new objects
steps.why: A model is only measured on things it has never seen. Twenty fresh trials is enough to see a pattern.
do: Open Teachable Machine. Your Day 2 project is usually still in the browser; if it's gone, retrain quickly with your same two classes.
Pick one class to be your 'positive'. Write it down.
Show the model 20 objects it has not seen before: 10 that are your positive, 10 that aren't. Change angles and backgrounds.
For each one, write two things: what the model said, and what was true.
steps.see: A list of 20 rows with a predicted label and an actual label. Some will disagree.
steps.tip: If the webcam button is grey, click the lock icon in the address bar and allow Camera.

checkpoint.prompt: I have 20 predicted-versus-actual results written down, 10 positive and 10 not.

steps.label: Build the confusion matrix in Sheets
steps.why: Four boxes turn 20 messy results into a picture of what kind of right and what kind of wrong.
do: Open sheets.google.com and start a blank sheet.
Type 'Actual Yes' in B1 and 'Actual No' in C1. Type 'Predicted Yes' in A2 and 'Predicted No' in A3.

Count your 20 results into the four cells: B2 is true positives (predicted yes, actual yes), C2 is false positives (predicted yes, actual no), B3 is false negatives (predicted no, actual yes), C3 is true negatives (predicted no, actual no).
In B4 type =B2+C2+B3+C3. It should say 20.
steps.see: A 2 by 2 grid of counts, and a cell under it showing 20.
steps.tip: If B4 doesn't say 20, one result was counted twice or not at all. Walk your 20 rows again.

checkpoint.prompt: The model said 'Mug' (your positive) but it was actually a phone. Which box does that go in?
checkpoint.why: It predicted yes (positive) and the truth was no. A false alarm is a false positive.

steps.label: Write the three formulas
steps.why: Typing the formula yourself is how the definitions stick. Reading them never does.
do: In A6 type 'Accuracy' and in B6 type =(B2+C3)/20. Right answers divided by everything.
In A7 type 'Precision' and in B7 type =B2/(B2+C2). Of everything it flagged, how many were right.
In A8 type 'Recall' and in B8 type =B2/(B2+B3). Of all the real positives, how many it caught.
Now change B2 down by one and B3 up by one. Watch which number moves most. Then change them back.
steps.see: Three decimals between 0 and 1. Moving one count from true positive to false negative drops recall a lot and accuracy only a little.

checkpoint.prompt: Type your three numbers (accuracy, precision, recall) and one sentence: which one moved most when you shifted a count, and why does that make sense?
checkpoint.placeholder: Accuracy 0.85, precision 0.9, recall 0.8. Recall moved most because I took a real positive the model used to catch and turned it into a miss, and recall only counts the real positives.

steps.label: Make three build-versus-buy calls
steps.why: The exam asks this constantly: does a ready-made service already do the job, or does the answer live only in your data?
do: For each problem, decide 'managed service' or 'custom model' and give one reason:

A) Pull text out of 5,000 scanned invoices. B) Predict which of your 300 regular customers will stop ordering next quarter, using your own sales history. C) Transcribe recorded customer calls to text.
Hint: a managed service fits common tasks (text from images, speech to text). A custom model fits problems only your data can answer.

checkpoint.prompt: Problem B (predict which of your 300 regular customers will stop ordering next quarter, from your own sales history) is best solved with:
options: A managed service like Amazon Textract
A managed service like Amazon Transcribe
A custom model trained on your data in SageMaker AI
checkpoint.why: No off-the-shelf service knows your customers. The answer lives only in your own history, so you build. Problems A and C are common tasks (text from documents, speech to text) with managed services ready: Textract and Transcribe.

steps.label: Share your sheet
do: Click Share in the top right of your Sheet. Change General access to 'Anyone with the link' as Viewer. Copy link.
Paste it below.
steps.see: Your link in the submissions list.

checkpoint.prompt: Link to your confusion matrix sheet

stretch: Pick a fraud or medical screening scenario and argue which metric matters most
Explain why high accuracy could still hide a dangerous model
doneWhen: A confusion matrix with working formulas

submission.prompt: Paste the link to your Google Sheet (set to anyone with the link can view).

lens.plain: The ten stages from business goal through data, training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring. Most of the work happens before training.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objective 1.3.1: describe and differentiate components of an AI/ML pipeline.

lens.plain: Keeping a deployed model alive: experimentation, repeatable processes, scalable systems, managing technical debt, production readiness, monitoring, and retraining when data drifts.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objective 1.3.5: fundamental concepts of ML operations.

lens.term: Confusion matrix; accuracy, precision, recall, F1
lens.plain: Four boxes (two ways right, two ways wrong). Accuracy is how often right; precision means few false alarms; recall means few missed cases; F1 balances the two.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objective 1.3.6: model performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score). AUC was dropped in exam guide v1.1.

lens.plain: Was the model worth building? Cost per user, development cost, customer feedback, return on investment.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objective 1.3.6: business metrics to evaluate ML models. Also Domain 2, Objective 2.2.4 for generative AI.

lens.term: Managed AWS AI services vs custom models
lens.plain: Buy a ready-made service for common jobs (Comprehend, Rekognition, Textract, Transcribe, Translate, Polly, Lex, Personalize). Build in SageMaker AI when only your own data has the answer. Bedrock, Quick, and Kiro cover other pipeline stages.
lens.exam: Domain 1, Objectives 1.2.5 (capabilities of managed AI/ML services), 1.3.4 (AWS services for each pipeline stage), and 1.3.2 (sources of models).

quiz.q: A cancer screening model misses 30% of real cases but never raises a false alarm. Which metric is low?
quiz.why: Recall measures how many real cases were caught. Missing 30% means recall is 70%.

quiz.q: Only 1 in 1,000 transactions is fraud. A model that says 'not fraud' every time scores 99.9% accuracy. Why is that dangerous?
a: It catches zero fraud; accuracy hides it because fraud is rare
quiz.why: When one class is rare, accuracy can look great while the model is useless. Recall on the rare class is what matters.

quiz.q: Which stage comes first in the ML lifecycle?
a: Collecting as much data as possible
quiz.why: The business goal decides what data you need, what success means, and which mistakes you can afford. Everything else follows from it.

quiz.q: A company wants to pull text out of scanned invoices and has no ML team. Best choice?
a: Train a custom model in SageMaker
Use a managed service like Amazon Textract
quiz.why: A managed service handles a common task out of the box. Custom models are for problems no ready-made service covers.

quiz.q: After a model is deployed, why does it still need monitoring?
a: Because real-world data can drift away from what the model trained on, so its performance decays
Because models get slower over time
Because the training data expires after 90 days
quiz.why: Data drift is the core reason. A fraud model trained on old patterns misses new ones. Monitoring catches the decay; retraining fixes it. That's the MLOps cycle.

cards.q: What comes first in an ML project, and why does it matter?
cards.a: The business goal. It decides what data you need, what success looks like, and which mistakes you can afford. Projects that start with 'we have data, let's do AI' usually fail.

cards.q: What are the stages of an ML pipeline, in order?
cards.a: Business goal, data collection, exploratory data analysis, preprocessing, feature engineering, training, tuning, evaluation, deployment, monitoring. Most of the effort is before training.
Looking at the data before modeling: charts, counts, distributions, surprises, missing values. It's how you find out whether the data can answer the question at all.
Shaping the clues the model will learn from: choosing, combining, or transforming raw inputs into useful signals. For example, turning a timestamp into 'day of week' and 'is holiday'.

The discipline of keeping a model alive in production: experimentation with tracking, repeatable processes, scalable systems, managing technical debt, production readiness, monitoring, and retraining.

cards.q: Why does a deployed model need monitoring and retraining?
cards.a: Because the world drifts. The data arriving today slowly stops looking like the data the model trained on, so its performance decays. Monitoring catches the decay; retraining on fresh data fixes it.

cards.q: Why can a 99.9% accurate model be useless?
cards.a: When the thing you care about is rare. If 1 in 1,000 transactions is fraud, a model that always says 'not fraud' is 99.9% accurate and catches nothing. Accuracy hides the failure.

cards.q: What are the four boxes of a confusion matrix?
cards.a: True positive (flagged it, and it was real), true negative (silent, and nothing there), false positive (a false alarm), false negative (a missed case). Every prediction lands in exactly one.
Of everything the model flagged as positive, how many really were. High precision means few false alarms. Formula: TP / (TP + FP).
Of all the real positives, how many the model caught. High recall means few missed cases. Formula: TP / (TP + FN). Medical screening and fraud detection usually care most about recall.

cards.q: What is the F1 score for?
cards.a: A single number that balances precision and recall, useful when you need both and the classes are imbalanced. It's the harmonic mean of the two, so one very low value drags it down.

cards.q: What are business metrics for an ML model, and how do they differ from model metrics?
cards.a: Model metrics say how well the model performs (accuracy, precision, recall). Business metrics say whether it was worth building: cost per user, development cost, customer feedback, return on investment.

cards.q: Which AWS managed service would you use to pull text and form fields out of scanned documents?
cards.a: Amazon Textract. Comprehend is for understanding text meaning and sentiment; Rekognition is for what's in images and video.

cards.q: Which AWS services handle speech, and in which direction?
cards.a: Amazon Transcribe turns speech into text. Amazon Polly turns text into speech. Amazon Lex builds the conversational bot that might use both.

cards.q: What do Amazon Comprehend, Translate, Rekognition, and Personalize each do?
cards.a: Comprehend reads text for meaning, entities, and sentiment. Translate translates between languages. Rekognition identifies objects, faces, and scenes in images and video. Personalize builds recommendation engines.

cards.q: What are the main sources of a model, and when do you pick each?
cards.a: Buy a managed service for common jobs. Borrow a pre-trained model (open source, or from SageMaker JumpStart) and adapt it. Build a custom model in SageMaker AI when the answer lives only in your own data.

cards.q: Which AWS service is the workbench for building, training, and deploying custom ML models?
cards.a: Amazon SageMaker AI. Inside it, Data Wrangler prepares data, Feature Store shares features, and JumpStart offers pre-trained models.

cards.q: How do Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Quick, and Kiro fit into an AI/ML pipeline?
cards.a: Bedrock gives access to foundation models when the job needs a large generative model instead of a custom one. Quick lets business users ask their data questions and build dashboards (it grew out of QuickSight). Kiro is AWS's AI coding tool for building the application around the model.

practice.q: A retail company's data team proposes starting an ML project by exporting every table in the data warehouse and 'seeing what the model finds.' According to the AI/ML lifecycle, what should happen first?
a: Collect more data from external sources
Define the business goal and how success will be measured
Choose between SageMaker AI and Bedrock
Deploy a prototype to get user feedback
practice.why: The business goal comes first. It determines what data matters, what metric defines success, and which errors are acceptable.
wrong: More data without a question is more noise.
Service choice is a deployment-stage decision.
You can't prototype toward an undefined goal.

practice.q: A data scientist is creating a 'days since last purchase' column from raw transaction timestamps before training a churn model. Which pipeline stage is this?
practice.why: Transforming raw inputs into useful signals for the model is feature engineering.
wrong: EDA is looking at the data, not building new inputs from it.
Evaluation happens after training, on held-out data.
Tuning adjusts the model's settings, not the data.

practice.q: A bank's fraud model performed well at launch but its detection rate has fallen steadily over eight months as fraud tactics changed. Which MLOps practice addresses this?
a: Monitor for data drift and retrain on recent data
Switch from real-time to batch inference
practice.why: Performance decay as the real world changes is data drift. Monitoring detects it; retraining on fresh data fixes it.
wrong: Changing a threshold doesn't teach the model new fraud patterns.
Inference mode affects speed and cost, not what the model knows.
Hyperparameters are tuning settings; they don't update the model's knowledge of the world.

practice.q: A hospital's screening model for a serious disease reports 97% accuracy. The disease affects 2% of patients. On review, the model identified only 40% of actual cases. Which metric best exposes this problem?
practice.why: Recall measures how many real positives were caught. 40% recall means 60% of sick patients were missed, which accuracy hides because most patients are healthy.
wrong: Accuracy is the number that looked fine and hid the problem.
Precision measures false alarms, not missed cases.
A business metric; it doesn't measure detection.

practice.q: An email provider wants its spam filter to almost never move a legitimate email to the spam folder, even if some spam gets through. Which metric should the team prioritize?
practice.why: Burying a real email is a false positive. Precision measures how many flagged emails were truly spam, so high precision means few false alarms.
wrong: Recall would prioritize catching all spam even at the cost of false alarms, the opposite of the goal.
Accuracy mixes both error types and can hide either.
Not a performance metric.

practice.q: A model produced these results on 100 test cases: 30 true positives, 10 false positives, 5 false negatives, 55 true negatives. What is its precision?
wrong: 0.86 is recall: 30 / (30 + 5), rounded.
0.30 is just the true positive count over 100.

practice.q: A company's recommendation model has excellent offline accuracy, but after launch, average revenue per user fell and support tickets rose. Which statement is MOST accurate?
a: The model is fine; business metrics are irrelevant to ML
The model metrics look good but the business metrics show it isn't delivering value
Accuracy must be wrong because revenue fell
The team should increase inference capacity
practice.why: Model metrics measure the model; business metrics (ROI, revenue per user, customer feedback) measure whether it was worth building. Here they disagree, and the business metrics win.
wrong: Business metrics are the point of the project.
Accuracy can be correct and the model still unhelpful to the business.
Capacity has nothing to do with a value problem.

practice.q: A logistics company receives 5,000 scanned paper invoices a month and wants to extract vendor names, dates, and totals automatically. It has no ML team. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
a: Train a custom computer vision model in SageMaker AI
practice.why: Textract is the managed service for extracting text and structured fields from documents. Common task, no ML team: buy.
wrong: Building a custom model for a solved, common task wastes months.
Comprehend analyzes the meaning of text you already have; it doesn't read scans.
Rekognition identifies objects and scenes in images, not document fields.

practice.q: Match the need to the service: a call center wants to convert recorded customer calls to text, then detect each caller's sentiment.
practice.why: Transcribe converts speech to text; Comprehend analyzes that text for sentiment.
wrong: Polly goes the other way (text to speech); Lex builds bots.
Rekognition is for images; Translate is for languages.
Textract reads documents; Personalize recommends products.

practice.q: A mid-size insurer wants to predict which of its own policyholders are likely to file a claim next year, using 15 years of internal claims history. Which approach fits BEST?
a: A custom model trained on the insurer's data in SageMaker AI
practice.why: The answer lives only in the insurer's own history; no managed service knows its policyholders. Build a custom model.
wrong: Personalize builds product recommendations, not risk predictions.
Comprehend analyzes text meaning.
Translate converts languages.

practice.q: A team wants to prepare and clean training data, store reusable features, and train a custom model, all within one AWS workbench. Which service?
practice.why: SageMaker AI is the end-to-end ML workbench; Data Wrangler and Feature Store live inside it.
wrong: Bedrock provides foundation models, not a custom-training workbench.
Quick is for asking business data questions and dashboards.
Kiro is an AI coding tool for building applications.

practice.q: A business analyst with no coding skills wants to ask questions of company sales data in plain English and get charts and reports. Which AWS service fits?
practice.why: Amazon Quick (the evolution of QuickSight) lets business users query data in natural language and build dashboards and reports.
wrong: SageMaker AI is a developer and data-scientist workbench.
Textract extracts text from documents.
AgentCore is infrastructure for running AI agents.

items.label: Confusion matrix sums to 20; metrics are live formulas
good: Your matrix adds up and the formulas are live, {name}, so the numbers move when the counts do.
Clean sheet, {name}. Four cells that sum to 20 and three real formulas.
fix: Some of your metric cells are typed numbers, not formulas. Click the cell: the bar should start with =.
Your three metrics should be formulas so they update. Retype them starting with = and test by changing a count.

items.label: Explains which metric moved most, and why
good: You explained why recall moved, {name}, not just that it did: "{quote}"
fix: Tell me why the number moved, not just which one. Recall only counts real positives, so turning a catch into a miss hits it hardest.
Your sentence names the metric but not the reason. What does recall count that accuracy doesn't?

items.label: Costlier mistake chosen and linked to precision or recall
good: You picked the costlier mistake before computing anything, {name}: "{quote}" That's the business-goal habit.
Good framing up front, {name}. You knew which mistake mattered before the numbers showed up.
fix: Connect your costlier mistake to a metric. If missed cases hurt more, recall is your number; if false alarms do, precision.
Say which metric your costlier mistake points to. That link is what the exam keeps asking about.

items.label: Three buy-or-build calls, each with a reason
good: Your buy-or-build reasons are sharp, {name}. You spotted that only your own data could answer the churn question.
All three calls are right and the reasons are the right ones, {name}.
fix: Add one reason to each buy-or-build call. The test is whether a ready-made service already does the job, or the answer lives only in your own data.
Each decision needs its why. 'Textract, because reading invoices is a common job' is the shape I'm after.
